title: Can subtraction give an angle without counting the marks?
description: Two arms pass through readings on the same protractor scale. Taking the smaller reading away from the larger one gives the angle between the arms, without counting every marking. Keeko's doubt, that the two readings are added, is broken by showing that the angle cannot be bigger than a reading itself.
teaching_notes: One idea: read both arms on the same scale and take the smaller reading away from the larger. Watch for the slip of adding the two readings.

source: Can you use the numbers marked to find the angle without cou
video_script.why: The child finds the angle between two arms by taking one reading away from the other on the same scale, instead of counting marks.
video_script.substitution: The gap between two readings is treated like the length between two marks on a ruler: take the smaller away from the larger.
video_script.anchor: the book's labelled protractor with the arms OT and OS passing through twenty and fifty five on the outer scale
video_script.wrong_answer: add twenty and fifty five to get seventy five degrees
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the two readings and says the angle is seventy five degrees. The angle is only the stretch between the two arms, which holds far fewer than seventy five units, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Fifty five take away twenty gives thirty five degrees

final_answer.spoken: yes, subtraction can be used, and fifty five take away twenty gives thirty five degrees

maths_rules: ground: a pencil with its ends at 14 and 40 on a ruler has length 40 - 14 = 26 units
arms OT and OS pass through 20 and 55 on the same outer set
the angle is the number of 1 degree units between them: 55 - 20 = 35, so the angle is 35 degrees
check: start at 20 and go up 35 units to reach 55
slip: adding gives 75, but 75 is more than the reading 55 itself, and the arms are only 35 units apart
video_script.design: One idea: take the smaller reading away from the larger on the same set. The ruler picture in the ground beat gives the child the subtraction idea before the protractor returns.
